Australia’s $30 billion base boom needs scrutiny too

While the billions of dollars Australia is spending on submarines, fighting vehicles, drones and jets receive plenty of attention, less well understood is the investment being made into Australia’s military bases.

Infrastructure might not seem that exciting. But these expensive weapons all need homes to go to.

Australia’s investment into the Defence estate is no less crucial to its “deter, shape, respond (Opens in new window)” objectives than its expanding navy or its guided weapons and explosive ordnance enterprise (Opens in new window).

The government is spending nearly $30 billion across four key sites: HMAS Stirling and Henderson in Western Australia, Osborne in South Australia, and RAAF Tindal in the Northern Territory.

Current satellite imagery offers a glimpse of what for most Australians are just names and a distance label on a map.

HMAS Stirling, 25/5/2022-10/03/2026 – wharves have been lengthened and new training facilities for submariners constructed.

HMAS Stirling, otherwise known as Fleet Base West, is the home of Australia’s submarine force. From 2027, it will host US and then UK nuclear-powered submarines as part of Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West). The government is investing $8 billion (Opens in new window) into the base to prepare it for the arrival of SRF-West, but renovation has been ongoing since at least 2018 (Opens in new window) to better serve the logistical requirements (Opens in new window) of Australia’s expanding surface fleet.

Since AUKUS was announced in 2021, the Oxley Wharf at the base has been extended, with Diamantia Wharf to be upgraded to accommodate nuclear-powered boats, and an extension to Parkes Wharf apparently shelved (Opens in new window). Shore facilities have been expanded to accommodate some 1000 US military personnel (Opens in new window) moving to the base, and the requirements involved in operating nuclear-powered submarines.

Osborne, 03/05/2022-25/09/2026 – the production demonstration workshop and skills and training academy are under construction, with preparatory work underway for further expansion from next year.

AUKUS is not just about military bases. Australia’s defence industry is seeing major cash injections as a result of the deal, particularly its submarine industry. The submarine yards at Osborne in South Australia will be central to Australia’s ambition to build its own nuclear boats by the 2040s and have received $8.5 billion (Opens in new window) of government investment.

Infrastructure might not seem that exciting. But these expensive weapons all need homes to go to.

Works at the site commenced in 2023, and cover three areas and a training campus (Opens in new window). Construction in Area 1, which will contain the yard’s fabrication hall, began in 2025. The main change visible from space is what will be Osborne’s production demonstration facilities, where building methods will be tested before turning to full-scale. Ground was broken in Area 2 in 2026, which will contain workshops and warehouses. Area 3, which will begin construction next year, is to the north of the complex and is where the new boats will be prepared in a consolidation hall before proceeding to a launching drydock. While the skills campus will open for students in 2028, Areas 1, 2, and 3 are estimated for completion in around 2035, 2036, and 2039 respectively.

The Henderson Defence Precinct south of Perth, Western Australia, will likewise be a key piece of infrastructure for Australia’s future navy. Australia is investing more than $12 billion (Opens in new window) in the site to greatly expand its role in continuous shipbuilding and sustainment, including for nuclear-powered submarines. While improvements have been made to the fabrication and support elements of the precinct, AUKUS-related construction is not yet being undertaken at Osborne. The boundaries (Opens in new window) of the new precinct were decided in August 2026 (Opens in new window), so major construction could begin next year. Indeed, if Australia is to receive its first nuclear-powered boat by the early 2030s (Opens in new window), construction of this sustainment facility must proceed at pace. Estimates are already suggesting costs will reach $25 billion (Opens in new window) over the next decade.

Henderson, 21/04/2022-13/10/2026 – small additions have been made but major work is yet to commence.

Not everything is about submarines. Aircraft also need lots of on-the-ground support. Australian air bases have been upgraded to play a greater role in hosting American forces. Canberra’s impulse to further integrate its defence with Washington goes beyond undersea warfare.

RAAF Tindal in the Northern Territory is a telling example. Since 2020, $1.6 billion (Opens in new window) has been invested to lengthen the runway, expand fuel and munitions storage (Opens in new window), build new hangars and command and control infrastructure. Tindal now hosts Australia’s growing fleet of Triton maritime surveillance drones (Opens in new window), and has runways long enough to land American B-52 bombers. Talks this week (Opens in new window) between Defence Minister Richard Marles and US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth emphasised a need to “swiftly” invest in Australian air force bases in a sign that the importance of facilities like Tindal will grow.

RAAF Tindall, 15/02/2022-19/09/2026 – the runway has been lengthened and several new hangars and storage facilities constructed.

How these installations grow and develop in the coming decade is vital to Australia’s defence strategy. While basing is not as exciting as submarines or aircraft, without places to be maintained and sustained, these weapons platforms cannot fulfil their roles. Given the amount of money involved in improving Australia’s defence infrastructure, these projects also require scrutiny.

By Russell Jackson

Topic:Cricket

Marques Ackerman's departure was another peculiar moment in the series. (AP: Halden Krog)

If there was any doubt how much the Cape Town Test matters to Pat Cummins's Australian team, one only needed to clock the cooing pack of them careening towards Cameron Green and Mitchell Starc an hour into the evening session of day three at Newlands.

The catch Green claimed to send his teammates into raptures was straightforward enough, its genesis and aftermath a little more dramatic.

Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, set fair on 62 and attacking everything Australia threw at him, had tried to limbo away from a Starc bouncer that followed him like a heat-seeking missile. Not quite agile enough with his Matrix manoeuvre, Ackerman faintly edged the ball flush into his faceguard, from which it ballooned into the cordon.

Unsure of the deflection and with his ears still ringing from the ding on his grill, Ackerman walked over to his skipper Temba Bavuma to discuss a review of the umpire's call, perhaps as surprised as the Australians when Travis Head arrived on the scene to inquire after his health.

But, in all the chaos and confusion, the crucial 15 seconds had passed before Ackerman could signal for a review. He had to depart.

It has been that sort of series, really; so many periods of ascendancy abruptly terminated by moments of genius, madness and confusion, and so many subversions of the pattern recognition Test cricket followers can normally rely on to impose a sense of order on what they're looking at.

South Africa finished the so-called moving day at 4-140 and 40 runs ahead. It would have wanted to be further in front. It could easily have been far worse off.

Earlier, in the latter stages of its first innings of 429, Australia probably let an extra 100 runs go begging. It sets up a perfect scenario even for those Australian fans who are not normally night owls: a thrilling finish on Friday night into Saturday morning.

On a pulsating day that produced 243 runs and 10 wickets, there was a second Test century for the recalled Josh Inglis and 80 for Alex Carey, both of whom fell to the off-spin of Simon Harmer.

In a Test featuring plenty of runs, only Josh Inglis has reached triple figures. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

An obscurity to most Australians before this series, and tipped to be dropped after the first Test, Harmer was in the thick of everything again with four wickets, two catches, a busted finger and plenty of chatter.

Youngster Cooper Connolly, looking entirely at home at Test level, made a patient 29 from 83 deliveries and might have kicked on further with better support from Australia's tail; the loss of 6-59 to finish off Australia's first innings was, as Pat Cummins often phrases such things, not ideal.

Yet it was still a 100-run lead, and early in South Africa's second innings you got the sense the game was about to break right open for an early finish.

In quick succession, Aiden Markram, who has been a thorn in Australia's side, lazily slapped a loose one from Starc into the clutches of Head at mid-off, and David Bedingham, seemingly rattled by a Starc bouncer that cannoned into his chest, holed out with another inexplicable hook.

The Proteas were 2-31, still 69 runs behind, and the hyenas were circling.

Via the counter-attack of Ackerman, then in a slow and steady partnership between Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke, South Africa began its rally. Yet there was one last twist in store with barely 15 minutes left in the day's play.

Having tortured Bavuma for a few hours with his sharp turn out of the footmarks, Nathan Lyon removed the Proteas skipper again, this time a dipping off break that snuck between bat and pad to castle the lunging batsman. Bavuma is not quite to Lyon what Daryll Cullinan once was to Shane Warne, but he is not far off.

Proteas captain Temba Bavuma posed a major threat to Australia. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

On the matter of hoodoos, much has been made in recent days of Cummins's record-breaking streak without a wicket.

It continued today, despite periods in which the Aussie skipper bowled with genuine pace and guile, although his desperation to break his drought was made clear by one ill-advised review. Even when it is 1.6 metre Bavuma in the firing line, it is always difficult to get an LBW call when it hits above the batsman's knee roll.

In truth, the odd brain fade was perfectly excusable due to the ratcheting up of the atmosphere as this game progressed.

Some testiness and conflict in this series was inevitable, but it has manifested in curious ways. Each team's most vocal player — Marnus Labuschagne for Australia, Matthew Breetzke for the Proteas — has been its worst performed.

Breetzke, in fact, finally started to come good late on day three, and will resume tomorrow believing he is the man to turn the game for his country.

Given the way these two teams have echoed each other's efforts in the past few weeks, perhaps that suggests one last tantalising and slightly mad prospect in the Australian chase: how about Marnus Labuschagne as the last-minute hero?

Australia’s $30 billion base boom needs scrutiny too

While the billions of dollars Australia is spending on submarines, fighting vehicles, drones and jets receive plenty of attention, less well understood is the investment being made into Australia’s military bases.

Infrastructure might not seem that exciting. But these expensive weapons all need homes to go to.

Australia’s investment into the Defence estate is no less crucial to its “deter, shape, respond (Opens in new window)” objectives than its expanding navy or its guided weapons and explosive ordnance enterprise (Opens in new window).

The government is spending nearly $30 billion across four key sites: HMAS Stirling and Henderson in Western Australia, Osborne in South Australia, and RAAF Tindal in the Northern Territory.

Current satellite imagery offers a glimpse of what for most Australians are just names and a distance label on a map.

HMAS Stirling, 25/5/2022-10/03/2026 – wharves have been lengthened and new training facilities for submariners constructed.

HMAS Stirling, otherwise known as Fleet Base West, is the home of Australia’s submarine force. From 2027, it will host US and then UK nuclear-powered submarines as part of Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West). The government is investing $8 billion (Opens in new window) into the base to prepare it for the arrival of SRF-West, but renovation has been ongoing since at least 2018 (Opens in new window) to better serve the logistical requirements (Opens in new window) of Australia’s expanding surface fleet.

Since AUKUS was announced in 2021, the Oxley Wharf at the base has been extended, with Diamantia Wharf to be upgraded to accommodate nuclear-powered boats, and an extension to Parkes Wharf apparently shelved (Opens in new window). Shore facilities have been expanded to accommodate some 1000 US military personnel (Opens in new window) moving to the base, and the requirements involved in operating nuclear-powered submarines.

Osborne, 03/05/2022-25/09/2026 – the production demonstration workshop and skills and training academy are under construction, with preparatory work underway for further expansion from next year.

AUKUS is not just about military bases. Australia’s defence industry is seeing major cash injections as a result of the deal, particularly its submarine industry. The submarine yards at Osborne in South Australia will be central to Australia’s ambition to build its own nuclear boats by the 2040s and have received $8.5 billion (Opens in new window) of government investment.

Infrastructure might not seem that exciting. But these expensive weapons all need homes to go to.

Works at the site commenced in 2023, and cover three areas and a training campus (Opens in new window). Construction in Area 1, which will contain the yard’s fabrication hall, began in 2025. The main change visible from space is what will be Osborne’s production demonstration facilities, where building methods will be tested before turning to full-scale. Ground was broken in Area 2 in 2026, which will contain workshops and warehouses. Area 3, which will begin construction next year, is to the north of the complex and is where the new boats will be prepared in a consolidation hall before proceeding to a launching drydock. While the skills campus will open for students in 2028, Areas 1, 2, and 3 are estimated for completion in around 2035, 2036, and 2039 respectively.

The Henderson Defence Precinct south of Perth, Western Australia, will likewise be a key piece of infrastructure for Australia’s future navy. Australia is investing more than $12 billion (Opens in new window) in the site to greatly expand its role in continuous shipbuilding and sustainment, including for nuclear-powered submarines. While improvements have been made to the fabrication and support elements of the precinct, AUKUS-related construction is not yet being undertaken at Osborne. The boundaries (Opens in new window) of the new precinct were decided in August 2026 (Opens in new window), so major construction could begin next year. Indeed, if Australia is to receive its first nuclear-powered boat by the early 2030s (Opens in new window), construction of this sustainment facility must proceed at pace. Estimates are already suggesting costs will reach $25 billion (Opens in new window) over the next decade.

Henderson, 21/04/2022-13/10/2026 – small additions have been made but major work is yet to commence.

Not everything is about submarines. Aircraft also need lots of on-the-ground support. Australian air bases have been upgraded to play a greater role in hosting American forces. Canberra’s impulse to further integrate its defence with Washington goes beyond undersea warfare.

RAAF Tindal in the Northern Territory is a telling example. Since 2020, $1.6 billion (Opens in new window) has been invested to lengthen the runway, expand fuel and munitions storage (Opens in new window), build new hangars and command and control infrastructure. Tindal now hosts Australia’s growing fleet of Triton maritime surveillance drones (Opens in new window), and has runways long enough to land American B-52 bombers. Talks this week (Opens in new window) between Defence Minister Richard Marles and US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth emphasised a need to “swiftly” invest in Australian air force bases in a sign that the importance of facilities like Tindal will grow.

RAAF Tindall, 15/02/2022-19/09/2026 – the runway has been lengthened and several new hangars and storage facilities constructed.

How these installations grow and develop in the coming decade is vital to Australia’s defence strategy. While basing is not as exciting as submarines or aircraft, without places to be maintained and sustained, these weapons platforms cannot fulfil their roles. Given the amount of money involved in improving Australia’s defence infrastructure, these projects also require scrutiny.

About the author

David Vallance

David Vallance is a Research Associate in the International Security Program at the Lowy Institute.

analysis

By Russell Jackson

Topic:Cricket

Marques Ackerman's departure was another peculiar moment in the series. (AP: Halden Krog)

If there was any doubt how much the Cape Town Test matters to Pat Cummins's Australian team, one only needed to clock the cooing pack of them careening towards Cameron Green and Mitchell Starc an hour into the evening session of day three at Newlands.

The catch Green claimed to send his teammates into raptures was straightforward enough, its genesis and aftermath a little more dramatic.

Proteas opener Marques Ackerman, set fair on 62 and attacking everything Australia threw at him, had tried to limbo away from a Starc bouncer that followed him like a heat-seeking missile. Not quite agile enough with his Matrix manoeuvre, Ackerman faintly edged the ball flush into his faceguard, from which it ballooned into the cordon.

Unsure of the deflection and with his ears still ringing from the ding on his grill, Ackerman walked over to his skipper Temba Bavuma to discuss a review of the umpire's call, perhaps as surprised as the Australians when Travis Head arrived on the scene to inquire after his health.

But, in all the chaos and confusion, the crucial 15 seconds had passed before Ackerman could signal for a review. He had to depart.

It has been that sort of series, really; so many periods of ascendancy abruptly terminated by moments of genius, madness and confusion, and so many subversions of the pattern recognition Test cricket followers can normally rely on to impose a sense of order on what they're looking at.

South Africa finished the so-called moving day at 4-140 and 40 runs ahead. It would have wanted to be further in front. It could easily have been far worse off.

Earlier, in the latter stages of its first innings of 429, Australia probably let an extra 100 runs go begging. It sets up a perfect scenario even for those Australian fans who are not normally night owls: a thrilling finish on Friday night into Saturday morning.

On a pulsating day that produced 243 runs and 10 wickets, there was a second Test century for the recalled Josh Inglis and 80 for Alex Carey, both of whom fell to the off-spin of Simon Harmer.

In a Test featuring plenty of runs, only Josh Inglis has reached triple figures. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

An obscurity to most Australians before this series, and tipped to be dropped after the first Test, Harmer was in the thick of everything again with four wickets, two catches, a busted finger and plenty of chatter.

Youngster Cooper Connolly, looking entirely at home at Test level, made a patient 29 from 83 deliveries and might have kicked on further with better support from Australia's tail; the loss of 6-59 to finish off Australia's first innings was, as Pat Cummins often phrases such things, not ideal.

Yet it was still a 100-run lead, and early in South Africa's second innings you got the sense the game was about to break right open for an early finish.

In quick succession, Aiden Markram, who has been a thorn in Australia's side, lazily slapped a loose one from Starc into the clutches of Head at mid-off, and David Bedingham, seemingly rattled by a Starc bouncer that cannoned into his chest, holed out with another inexplicable hook.

The Proteas were 2-31, still 69 runs behind, and the hyenas were circling.

Via the counter-attack of Ackerman, then in a slow and steady partnership between Temba Bavuma and Matthew Breetzke, South Africa began its rally. Yet there was one last twist in store with barely 15 minutes left in the day's play.

Having tortured Bavuma for a few hours with his sharp turn out of the footmarks, Nathan Lyon removed the Proteas skipper again, this time a dipping off break that snuck between bat and pad to castle the lunging batsman. Bavuma is not quite to Lyon what Daryll Cullinan once was to Shane Warne, but he is not far off.

Proteas captain Temba Bavuma posed a major threat to Australia. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

On the matter of hoodoos, much has been made in recent days of Cummins's record-breaking streak without a wicket.

It continued today, despite periods in which the Aussie skipper bowled with genuine pace and guile, although his desperation to break his drought was made clear by one ill-advised review. Even when it is 1.6 metre Bavuma in the firing line, it is always difficult to get an LBW call when it hits above the batsman's knee roll.

In truth, the odd brain fade was perfectly excusable due to the ratcheting up of the atmosphere as this game progressed.

Some testiness and conflict in this series was inevitable, but it has manifested in curious ways. Each team's most vocal player — Marnus Labuschagne for Australia, Matthew Breetzke for the Proteas — has been its worst performed.

Breetzke, in fact, finally started to come good late on day three, and will resume tomorrow believing he is the man to turn the game for his country.

Given the way these two teams have echoed each other's efforts in the past few weeks, perhaps that suggests one last tantalising and slightly mad prospect in the Australian chase: how about Marnus Labuschagne as the last-minute hero?
